items.summary_en:
Contrary to popular perception, most people will not adopt a new technology just because it makes them more efficient.

Instead, they’ll adopt new technology because:
- Someone they know who’s similar to them on some dimension adopted the technology, and got positive results (eg became cooler, richer, more popular/respected), and they wanna become like that person 
- They feel like everyone around them has adopted the technology, and if they don’t, they’ll be left behind

Notice that it’s not entirely a rational decision. It’s more of an EMOTIONAL decision.

So if you’re trying to make someone adopt a new technology, the messaging shouldn’t be “this will make you 10x more efficient!” It should be “So-and-so, someone you can relate to, has adopted this and look how much better their life has become; wouldn’t it be nice to be like them?”

This book reminds you of that. It can be distilled in one sentence: “The diffusion of technology is a SOCIAL process”
items.summary_zh:
人们采用新技术很少是因为“效率提升 10 倍”这种理性卖点，而是因为看到和自己相似的人用了之后变酷、变有钱、变受尊重，或者害怕自己不跟上就会掉队。

技术扩散本质上不是效率竞赛，而是一场社会模仿和情绪驱动的传染。

items.author: Aaron Levie
items.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
items.summary_en:
One fun benefit of spending so much time with enterprises is you get to see the array of AI implementation strategies that exist in companies right now. 

Unlike the early innings of cloud where there were really only a couple deployment patterns available -including being limited by only a couple infra vendors existing- AI actually has a much wider range of approaches in the enterprise.

If you ask 10 IT leaders what their coding agent strategy looks like, you get at least 5 different answers. If you ask about their end-user productivity agents, some have standardized on ChatGPT or Claude, others offer a choice of multiple solutions, and many have built their own orchestration layers for employees to use any model. 

For models, we know the big ones, but increasingly enterprises are experimenting with OSS models, or are at least immensely curious about OSS and would jump at the right offering that felt safe. And increasingly there’s a set of vertical models and agents that equally show up in enterprises for a range of tailored use-cases.

For accessing data, some enterprises just have agents take on the role of the user, and others are setting up agent users that have their own identities. Some companies are setting up substantial guardrails on what agents can do, and others are putting responsibility on the user.

Given this heterogeneity this early on at the start, it means we’re in for years of landscape changes. Anyone who’s predicting ultimate market outcomes already probably will be wrong as nothing has formally settled in yet. Lots of opportunity ahead.
items.summary_zh:

现在就断言最终赢家基本是在赌运气，因为企业 AI 的格局还没凝固，接下来几年会持续洗牌。

Ok builders, here’s your playbook. 

Prototype your product with the best frontier model. Cost be damned. 
Validate the user experience.

Then, 6-8 weeks later when open-weight models catch up - move your production workloads there, and to smaller models where possible.

In that order. Don’t start with the cheapest model.

items.summary_en:
.@TryRivo is building self-driving finance.

Agents connect to the checking account you already have, learn your cash flow, sweep dollars into Treasury-backed yield, and bring them back before your bills hit.

Every dollar earns until the moment you spend it.

Why is this hard? Prediction under asymmetric cost.

Money returned a day early costs you a little yield. 

Money returned a day late bounces a bill and destroys trust.

@AmbrishTweets is one of the few people who has shipped this class of system before. 

PhD in AI, 7,000+ citations, built consumer AI at Amazon, and led the L4 autonomy work at Cruise that launched robotaxis, before he came through @spc as a Founder Fellow.

Self-driving cars took two decades because the last edge cases were the hard ones.

Self-driving money is the same problem with a friendlier failure mode, and the founder building it has already solved the harder version once.
items.summary_zh:
Rivo 在做“自动驾驶金融”：AI 代理接入你的活期账户，预测现金流，把闲钱扫进美国国债收益里，并在账单扣款前拉回来，让每一美元在花掉前都持续赚钱。

难点不是转账，而是不对称成本下的预测：早一天回来只是少赚点收益，晚一天回来就是账单跳票、信任崩塌；创始人 Ambrish 做过 Cruise L4 自动驾驶，等于把更难的边缘情况打过一遍。

items.author: Madhu Guru
items.bio: Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.
items.summary_en:
The best model for early product validation is almost never the best model for production.

Talked to a bunch of founders this weekend. There’s a standard playbook emerging :

1/ Prototype with the best frontier models. Max quality. Ignore cost and latency.
Learn what users actually want and iterate. 

2/ Once the workflow and UX is validated, optimize like crazy for cost and latency - prompt eng, model routing, harnesses, smaller models, fine tuning. 

I see most teams get stuck in step 1.
items.summary_zh: 早期验证要用最强模型，不管成本和延迟，先把用户真正想要什么跑出来。真正的分水岭在第二步：体验验证后疯狂压成本、降延迟，而大多数团队卡死在“原型很酷”这一步。

How to judge if a meeting is efficient:

An efficient meeting has no to-do list left behind, because all the actions are done DURING the meeting (either by agents who listen to the meeting in real time or by humans)

The gap between saying and doing should be zero, and meetings become work sessions where things actually get DONE
items.summary_zh:
高效会议不是会后留下一堆待办，而是所有动作在会中就被完成，无论靠实时听会的 agent 还是人。

说完和做完之间的间隙应该是 0；会议不该是同步进展，而该是直接把事干掉。

items.author: Training Data
items.title: Chai Discovery's Bitter Lesson: Drug Design Is Another Scaling Problem
items.summary_en:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:22
One of our big guiding principles is just simplicity. So, like, when you look at a model like, let's say, CHI one, I think there are 23 distinct submodules in CHI one. And, like, when you're trying to iterate on something like that, it gets really hard because you're like, I kinda I need to understand each of these sub modules independently. I need to understand all of their behaviors, their dynamics, and, like, that doesn't actually scale that well. So, like, you can start to think, okay.

Speaker 1 | 00:22 - 00:31
How do I simplify this? How do I identify, like, what's what's really important? Once you have that, the whole research process and identifying these types of scaling directions becomes a lot simpler.

Speaker 2 | 00:48 - 01:01
We're here with Josh and Matt, two of the co founders of CHI Discovery. CHI is engineering molecules with AI. So it's something of a foundation model lab for biology. Sounds like a big idea, but let

Speaker 3 | 01:01 - 01:25
me just start there. What is the big idea? Thanks for having us on the show. One of the exciting things we're trying to do at CHI is to make the drug discovery process look a little bit more like engineering, and we've seen all the work happening with the LMs for cogeneration, for instance, right, and that works really well because code's a very simple obstruction, right, of like to kind of get across what you want to do. Biology doesn't look like that today.

Speaker 3 | 01:25 - 01:52
It's a lot of like trial and error. I think if we go back to the early days of just like modern biotech, right, a lot of the medicines that we have today were kind of discovered quite randomly. It was a bit serendipitous, and what we're trying to do is allow us to industrialize that process a little bit mo
items.summary_zh: Chai Discovery 的核心判断很硬：药物发现不是玄学，也不该靠撞大运，它最终会被压成一个可工程化、可规模化的问题。模型越复杂越难迭代，真正的突破反而来自把系统简化到能看清哪些东西在驱动 scaling。
